newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Malan in court for murder case verdict.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Malan in court for murder case verdict.

text.p: Former defence minister Magnus Malan, the most senior figure charged with apartheid-era atrocities against blacks, awaited the verdict on Thursday in his seven-month trial for murder.
The ruling began with a fierce attack by Judge Jan Hugo on the prosecution case, based on three witnesses he referred to as "self-confessed criminals".

Malan and 15 co-defendants face 13 counts of murder for a death squad attack on the family of a black activist nine years ago. The case is South Africa's biggest trial to date of apartheid-era human rights abuses.

The defendants sat in the supreme court in the Indian Ocean port of Durban, near the township scene of the massacre, as Hugo began to read what was expected to be a lengthy verdict, possibly taking up to two days.
Hugo said he would rule first on the six accused of carrying out the attack, for which Malan and the others are blamed.
He attacked the prosecution case against them, casting doubt on the reliability of the three witnesses called by the state.
The court had to be aware they were "self-confessed criminals who are trying to get some benefits by testifying... red lights must necessarily start flashing", Hugo said.
"We would have greatly doubted their veracity, even if they were not accomplices," he added, reading from his judgment.
The defendants appeared encouraged by his opening remarks.
Malan is the highest-ranking member of the old apartheid government to be charged with abuses committed to maintain white minority rule over the black majority.
He and the others accused have repeatedly declared their innocence during the trial.

Malan, head of the armed forces before he entered the cabinet, admits he helped set up a paramilitary force for the Zulu-based Inkatha party, the main black rival of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress.
But he says the force was legitimate and that if it had any hand in the massacre of seven adults and six young children, he knew nothing about it.
Acquittal would be welcomed by supporters of the old government, who have called the trial a witch hunt.

Those who suffered under apartheid say a not-guilty verdict for Malan, who led the white government's war against black opponents, would deal a heavy setback to South Africa's efforts to punish the crimes of the past.
Co-defendants include six Zulu police accused of carrying out the attack, a top Inkatha official, three generals, two majors, a vice-admiral, a brigadier and a senior policeman.
Four of the original 20 accused were acquitted earlier because of lack of evidence against them.

Judge Hugo also criticised the methods of the investigation, saying some evidence was probably "deliberately misleading" and that the prosecution had failed to call numerous witnesses who might have been able to shed light on the affair.

Malan, accused number 19, wore a blue suit with a striped white and blue shirt. He leaned over and took notes during the proceedings, seated alongside the other defendants on cushioned chairs in a raised dock in the colonial-style wood-panelled courtroom.
Also in court was the mother of Victor Ntuli, the activist who was the intended target of the 1987 massacre in which his relatives were killed.
He survived the attack, only to be murdered a few years later by persons unknown.
